messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus T.

Marcus had been working construction for seventeen years without incident. He was the kind of man who showed up early, knew his way around a site, and could talk any crew through a problem. On a Tuesday in March, he was supervising the demolition of an old apartment building downtown when the crane operator—a guy named David who'd been on the job for three weeks—made a miscalculation with the load. Marcus watched from thirty feet away as the steel beam twisted, the cable snapped, and David fell. He hit the pavement hard enough that Marcus heard it over the ambient noise of the site. The smell was immediate: dust, concrete, and something acrid that Marcus would later realize was fear-sweat mixed with blood. He was the first to reach David, whose body was already wrong in ways Marcus's mind couldn't quite process. David's eyes were open, and then they weren't. Marcus spent the next two hours sitting in a police car, his clothes still dusty, tasting copper and bile in his mouth.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus couldn't stop seeing David's face—not as it had been that morning, but as it was in those final seconds. The images came unbidden: a snapshot, then another, each one vivid and intrusive. When he tried to sleep, his mouth would fill with that metallic taste, and the smell of dust would cut through the darkness of his bedroom. His wife, Patricia, would find him staring at nothing, his jaw clenched. She asked what was wrong. He said he was fine. He wasn't fine. The images and sensations kept returning, and each time they did, Marcus felt something shift in how he understood the world. He had always believed that if you worked hard and stayed alert, you could prevent bad things. But he had been alert. He had been right there. And David had died anyway. The randomness of it—the fact that the crane operator had been new, that the cable had been old, that Marcus happened to be standing in exactly the right place to see it all—began to feel less like accident and more like evidence that nothing he did mattered. He was inadequate to protect anyone, including himself. Bad things happened, and there was nothing he could do to stop them.

Marcus found himself unable to tolerate the weight of these thoughts. When the images surfaced—David's open eyes, the twisted beam—he would feel a surge of anger that frightened him more than the memories themselves. He was angry at David for being careless, at the company for hiring him, at himself for being there. But he had also been taught as a boy that anger was something men should never show, something that led to losing control. So instead of letting it out, Marcus pushed it down. He swallowed it. He went to a casino one evening in May, telling himself he just needed a break, and found that the bright lights and the sound of slot machines and the small rush of placing bets could pull him away from his own mind for hours. He'd return home at two in the morning, his shirt damp, his hands shaking slightly, and Patricia would ask where he'd been. He'd say work ran late. The gambling became weekly, then twice weekly. He'd lose money he couldn't afford to lose, but the moment of placing a bet—that split second of possibility before the outcome was determined—felt like the only time he wasn't trapped inside his own head.

When the images came at work, Marcus developed a different strategy. He learned to dissociate, to deliberately step outside his body and let his mind go blank. He'd be standing on a scaffold, and he'd let his thoughts scatter like smoke, his eyes unfocused. His foreman noticed he was slower, less sharp. There were near-misses. Patricia filed for divorce in August; she said she didn't recognize him anymore, that he was never really home even when he was there. Marcus didn't fight her on it. He couldn't explain that he was fighting just to keep himself functioning, that every moment required him to either blank out or gamble or suppress the rage that threatened to consume him. The intrusive sensations—the taste, the smell, the images—had convinced him that he was helpless against his own mind, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that he himself was inadequate to face any of it. By October, he had burned through most of his savings at the casino, his work performance had deteriorated enough that his boss had put him on probation, and he was drinking most nights to help the dissociation along. It was only when his ex-wife's lawyer sent him a letter about back child support that Marcus finally called a therapist. He was exhausted. He wanted to know if there was any way to make the memories stop, and whether there was any point in trying to change when the world had already proven itself to be completely unpredictable and hostile.
